sources: DISA STIG — Active Directory Domain and Active Directory Forest
Microsoft — Best Practices for Securing Active Directory
MITRE ATT&CK — Enterprise, Credential Access / Privilege Escalation / Persistence
ManageEngine ADManager Plus — Identity Security Risk Assessment (contraste, no copia)
Purple Knight — Security Assessment (contraste, no copia)

indicators.title: Enabled user accounts have a password that never expires

remediation.summary: Remove 'Password never expires' from interactive accounts and move service accounts to gMSAs.
steps: Separate the list into people and service accounts.
For people, clear 'Password never expires' so the domain password policy applies.
For services, migrate to group Managed Service Accounts; document any remaining exception with an owner and expiry.
remediation.risk: A service account whose password starts expiring stops its service when the password ages out.

references.title: Valid Accounts: Domain Accounts
Active Directory Domain STIG — password expiration

indicators.title: User accounts store their password with reversible encryption

remediation.summary: Clear 'Store password using reversible encryption' and force a password change on every listed account.
steps: Uncheck the option on each account (or Set-ADUser -AllowReversiblePasswordEncryption $false).
Require the user to change the password at next logon — the reversible copy stays until the password changes.
Verify the Default Domain Policy does not enable reversible encryption.
remediation.risk: Applications using CHAP or digest authentication that depend on reversible passwords stop working.

references.title: OS Credential Dumping
Active Directory Domain STIG — reversible password encryption

indicators.title: Enabled user accounts are allowed to have an empty password

remediation.summary: Clear the PASSWD_NOTREQD flag on every listed account and set a compliant password.
steps: Run Set-ADAccountControl -PasswordNotRequired $false for each account.
Set a password that meets the domain policy if the account currently has none.
remediation.risk: An account that really had no password stops authenticating until one is set.

references.title: Valid Accounts: Domain Accounts

indicators.title: Enabled user accounts have not signed in for more than 180 days

remediation.summary: Disable accounts that are no longer used and remove them after a holding period.
steps: Confirm with each account's owner or HR that the account is no longer needed.
Disable the account and move it to a quarantine OU.
Delete it after the organization's retention period.
remediation.risk: lastLogonTimestamp replicates with up to 14 days of lag; an account used only against a single DC may look stale when it is not.

references.title: Valid Accounts: Domain Accounts
Active Directory Domain STIG — inactive accounts

indicators.title: Objects carry SID history

remediation.summary: Finish the migration that created the SID history, re-permission resources with current SIDs and clear sIDHistory.
steps: Find resources still granting access to the old SIDs.
Replace those ACEs with the object's current SID or group.
Clear the sIDHistory attribute on each listed object.
remediation.risk: Clearing SID history before re-permissioning removes access that users still depend on.

references.title: Access Token Manipulation: SID-History Injection

indicators.title: The built-in Administrator password is older than 365 days

remediation.summary: Rotate the built-in Administrator password, keep it in a vault and use named admin accounts day to day.
steps: Set a long random password on the built-in Administrator (RID 500).
Store it in the organization's privileged access vault with break-glass procedure.
Use individual administrative accounts for daily work.
remediation.risk: Scheduled tasks or services still running as Administrator stop working after the change.

references.title: Valid Accounts: Default Accounts

indicators.title: The built-in Guest account is enabled

remediation.summary: Disable the built-in Guest account.
steps: Run Disable-ADAccount -Identity Guest, or disable it in 'Active Directory Users and Computers'.
remediation.risk: None expected; nothing supported should depend on the domain Guest account.

references.title: Valid Accounts: Default Accounts
Active Directory Domain STIG — Guest account

indicators.title: Privileged accounts have a password older than 365 days

remediation.summary: Reset the password of every privileged account that has not changed it in over a year, and put those accounts on a rotation.
steps: Confirm each account is a real privileged account and not a decommissioned one.
Reset its password and, for service accounts, prefer a group Managed Service Account so rotation is automatic.
remediation.risk: A privileged password that never changes is a long-lived target for offline cracking; rotating a service account's password without updating the service breaks it.

references.title: Valid Accounts: Domain Accounts

indicators.title: Anonymous LDAP operations are enabled (dSHeuristics)

remediation.summary: Set the seventh character of dSHeuristics back to 0 (or clear the attribute if nothing else is set).
steps: Open ADSI Edit on the Configuration partition › CN=Services › CN=Windows NT › CN=Directory Service.
Change the seventh character of dSHeuristics from 2 to 0, keeping the other characters.
Confirm no application depends on anonymous binds before the change.
remediation.risk: Applications that read the directory anonymously stop working.

references.title: Account Discovery: Domain Account
dSHeuristics attribute

indicators.title: Any authenticated user can join computers to the domain (ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota > 0)

remediation.summary: Set ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota to 0 and delegate computer joins to a dedicated group.
steps: Delegate 'Create Computer objects' on the target OUs to the team that joins machines.
Set ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota to 0 on the domain object.
remediation.risk: Users who join their own machines today can no longer do it without the delegated group.

references.title: Default limit to number of workstations a user can join to the domain
Create Account: Domain Account

indicators.title: The forest functional level is below Windows Server 2016

remediation.summary: Raise the domain and forest functional levels once every DC runs Windows Server 2016 or later.
steps: Confirm every domain controller in the forest runs Windows Server 2016 or newer.
Raise each domain functional level, then the forest functional level (Set-ADForestMode).
remediation.risk: Raising the functional level is not reversible below the new level; older DCs can no longer be added.

references.title: Active Directory Domain Services functional levels

indicators.title: The domain password policy allows passwords shorter than 14 characters

remediation.summary: Raise 'Minimum password length' in the Default Domain Policy to 14.
steps: Edit the Default Domain Policy › Computer Configuration › Policies › Windows Settings › Security Settings › Account Policies › Password Policy.
Set 'Minimum password length' to 14 characters.
Communicate the change: existing passwords keep working until their next change.
remediation.risk: Users are forced into longer passwords at their next change; help-desk volume rises briefly.

references.title: Active Directory Domain STIG — minimum password length
Brute Force

indicators.title: LAPS is not deployed (no LAPS attribute in the schema)

remediation.summary: Deploy Windows LAPS so every local administrator password is unique and rotated.
steps: Extend the schema with Update-LapsADSchema.
Grant computers permission to update their password (Set-LapsADComputerSelfPermission) on the target OUs.
Enable the LAPS policy through Group Policy or Intune.
remediation.risk: Local administrator passwords change; scripts that use a shared local password stop working.

references.title: Windows LAPS overview
Use Alternate Authentication Material: Pass the Hash

indicators.title: Group Policy Preferences in SYSVOL contain stored passwords (cpassword)

remediation.summary: Delete the preference items that store passwords and change every password they contained.
steps: Open each reported GPO and remove the preference item that sets a password.
Change the password of every account those items configured — the key that encrypts cpassword is public.
Replace local account management with Windows LAPS.
remediation.risk: Machines stop receiving the account or mapping the preference item configured.

references.title: MS14-025: Vulnerability in Group Policy Preferences
Unsecured Credentials: Group Policy Preferences

indicators.title: Fine-grained password policies allow passwords shorter than 14 characters

remediation.summary: Raise msDS-MinimumPasswordLength to 14 on every password settings object.
steps: Open 'Active Directory Administrative Center' › System › Password Settings Container.
Set 'Minimum password length' to at least 14 on each listed object.
remediation.risk: Members of the affected policy must choose longer passwords at their next change.

references.title: Fine-grained password policies

indicators.title: Outbound trusts to external domains do not filter SID history

remediation.summary: Enable SID filtering (quarantine) on external trusts unless a documented migration still needs SID history.
steps: Confirm no migration in progress relies on SID history across the trust.
Enable quarantine: netdom trust <TrustingDomain> /domain:<TrustedDomain> /quarantine:Yes.
remediation.risk: Users that rely on SID history from the trusted domain lose access to resources in this domain.

references.title: Access Token Manipulation: SID-History Injection
Active Directory Forest STIG — SID filtering on external trusts

indicators.title: The domain does not lock out accounts after repeated failed sign-ins

remediation.summary: Set an account lockout threshold between 1 and 10 failed attempts in the Default Domain Policy.
steps: Open the Default Domain Policy: Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Account Policies > Account Lockout Policy.
Set 'Account lockout threshold' to a value between 1 and 10 (for example 5), with a lockout duration and observation window.
remediation.risk: No lockout allows unlimited password guessing; too low a threshold makes it easy for an attacker to lock out users on purpose (denial of service).

references.title: Account lockout threshold

indicators.title: The forest functional level is below Windows Server 2012

remediation.summary: Raise the forest functional level to at least Windows Server 2012 to enable modern protections (for example the Protected Users group and Authentication Policies need 2012 R2).
steps: Confirm every domain controller runs Windows Server 2012 or later.
Raise each domain functional level, then the forest functional level (Set-ADForestMode).
remediation.risk: Raising the functional level is not reversible below the new level and blocks adding older domain controllers.

references.title: Active Directory Domain Services functional levels

indicators.title: The domain controller does not require LDAP signing

remediation.summary: Require LDAP signing on every domain controller.
steps: Enable LDAP Interface Events (diagnostics level 2) and review event 2889 to find clients that bind without signing.
Fix or reconfigure those clients.
Set 'Domain controller: LDAP server signing requirements' to 'Require signing' in the Default Domain Controllers Policy.
remediation.gpoPath: Computer Configuration › Policies › Windows Settings › Security Settings › Local Policies › Security Options › Domain controller: LDAP server signing requirements
remediation.risk: Clients that bind with simple or unsigned SASL binds fail until they are reconfigured.

references.title: How to enable LDAP signing in Windows Server
Adversary-in-the-Middle

indicators.title: The domain controller does not enforce LDAP channel binding

remediation.summary: Enforce LDAP channel binding tokens on every domain controller.
steps: Set LdapEnforceChannelBinding to 1 and review event 3039 for clients that fail.
Update or reconfigure those clients.
Set LdapEnforceChannelBinding to 2 ('Always').
remediation.risk: LDAPS clients that do not support channel binding tokens fail to bind.

references.title: ADV190023: LDAP channel binding and LDAP signing

indicators.title: SMBv1 is enabled on the domain controller

remediation.summary: Disable SMBv1 on the domain controller.
steps: Check the SMB1 access audit (Set-SmbServerConfiguration -AuditSmb1Access $true, event 3000) for clients still using SMBv1.
Run Set-SmbServerConfiguration -EnableSMB1Protocol $false, or remove the SMB1Protocol feature.
remediation.risk: Legacy devices that only speak SMBv1 lose access to SYSVOL and NETLOGON.

references.title: How to detect, enable and disable SMBv1, SMBv2, and SMBv3
Exploitation of Remote Services

indicators.title: The Print Spooler service is not disabled on the domain controller

remediation.summary: Stop and disable the Print Spooler service on domain controllers.
steps: Confirm the DC is not used as a print server.
Run Stop-Service Spooler; Set-Service Spooler -StartupType Disabled.
remediation.risk: Printers shared from the domain controller stop working.

references.title: CVE-2021-34527 Windows Print Spooler Remote Code Execution
Forced Authentication

indicators.title: The domain controller accepts LM and NTLMv1 responses (LmCompatibilityLevel below 5)

remediation.summary: Set 'Network security: LAN Manager authentication level' to 'Send NTLMv2 response only. Refuse LM & NTLM'.
steps: Audit NTLMv1 use (event 4624 with 'Package Name (NTLM only): NTLM V1').
Fix the clients still using NTLMv1.
Set the policy in the Default Domain Controllers Policy.
remediation.gpoPath: Computer Configuration › Policies › Windows Settings › Security Settings › Local Policies › Security Options › Network security: LAN Manager authentication level
remediation.risk: Clients limited to LM or NTLMv1 can no longer authenticate against this DC.

references.title: Windows Server STIG — LAN Manager authentication level
Adversary-in-the-Middle

indicators.title: UAC admin approval mode is disabled for the built-in Administrator on the domain controller

remediation.summary: Enable 'User Account Control: Admin Approval Mode for the Built-in Administrator account' on domain controllers.
steps: Set the policy in Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options.
This sets FilterAdministratorToken to 1 under the Policies\\System key.
remediation.risk: With Admin Approval Mode off, code run by the built-in Administrator gets a full token with no elevation prompt; a script that relied on silent elevation may now prompt.

references.title: UAC: Admin Approval Mode for the Built-in Administrator account

indicators.title: The domain controller stores the LAN Manager hash of passwords

remediation.summary: Prevent domain controllers from storing the LAN Manager hash of passwords.
steps: Set 'Network security: Do not store LAN Manager hash value on next password change' to Enabled in the Default Domain Controllers Policy.
Every account's LM hash is removed at its next password change.
remediation.risk: The LM hash is trivially crackable; disabling it can break very old clients that only speak LM authentication.

references.title: Do not store LAN Manager hash value on next password change

indicators.title: The krbtgt account password has not been reset in the last 180 days

remediation.summary: Reset the krbtgt password twice, waiting for replication (at least the maximum ticket lifetime, 10 hours by default) between resets.
steps: Confirm AD replication is healthy on every DC (repadmin /replsummary).
Reset the krbtgt password once with the Microsoft New-KrbtgtKeys.ps1 script or 'Active Directory Users and Computers'.
Wait at least the maximum Kerberos ticket lifetime plus replication latency.
Reset it a second time so tickets forged with the old key stop being accepted.
remediation.risk: Resetting twice without waiting invalidates every issued Kerberos ticket at once and causes authentication failures until clients re-authenticate.

references.title: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: Golden Ticket
AD Forest Recovery — Resetting the krbtgt password

indicators.title: Privileged accounts have a service principal name (Kerberoastable)

remediation.summary: Remove SPNs from privileged user accounts; run services under group Managed Service Accounts instead.
steps: For each listed account, identify the service that registered the SPN (setspn -L <account>).
Move the service to a gMSA or a non-privileged service account with a long random password.
Remove the SPN from the privileged account (setspn -D <spn> <account>).
remediation.risk: Removing an SPN that is still in use breaks Kerberos authentication to that service.

references.title: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: Kerberoasting
Active Directory Domain STIG — privileged account usage

indicators.title: Enabled accounts do not require Kerberos pre-authentication (AS-REP roastable)

remediation.summary: Clear 'Do not require Kerberos preauthentication' on every listed account.
steps: Open each account in 'Active Directory Users and Computers' › Account.
Uncheck 'Do not require Kerberos preauthentication', or run Set-ADAccountControl -DoesNotRequirePreAuth $false.
If a legacy application needs it, document an exception with an expiry date.
remediation.risk: Very old Kerberos clients that cannot do pre-authentication stop authenticating.

references.title: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: AS-REP Roasting

indicators.title: Accounts other than domain controllers are trusted for unconstrained delegation

remediation.summary: Replace unconstrained delegation with constrained or resource-based constrained delegation.
steps: For each listed object, identify which service needs to delegate and to which back-end service.
Configure constrained delegation to only those services (Delegation tab › 'Trust this computer for delegation to specified services only').
Clear 'Trust this computer for delegation to any service'.
remediation.risk: Applications that rely on delegation to unlisted back-ends fail with double-hop authentication errors.

references.title: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets
Kerberos constrained delegation overview

indicators.title: Accounts are trusted for constrained delegation with protocol transition

remediation.summary: Remove protocol transition (TRUSTED_TO_AUTH_FOR_DELEGATION) from accounts that do not require it, or move to resource-based constrained delegation.
steps: Review each account and the services it delegates to (msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo).
Where possible replace 'Use any authentication protocol' with 'Use Kerberos only', or migrate to resource-based constrained delegation configured on the target.
Never grant protocol transition to a Tier 0 service account.
remediation.risk: Protocol transition lets the account request tickets for any user to the configured services; removing it breaks front-ends that rely on it (for example some Kerberos-constrained-delegation web apps).

references.title: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: Kerberoasting

indicators.title: Accounts with a service principal name allow RC4 or weaker Kerberos encryption

remediation.summary: Configure every service account with a service principal name to support AES Kerberos encryption.
steps: For each account, set msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes to AES128+AES256 (value 24) once the target services support AES.
Reset the account password so AES keys are generated.
Prefer group Managed Service Accounts, which use AES by default and rotate their own password.
remediation.risk: An RC4-only service ticket is offline-crackable (Kerberoasting); forcing AES before a legacy service supports it breaks that service.

references.title: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: Kerberoasting
Decrypting the Selection of Supported Kerberos Encryption Types

indicators.title: Accounts are enabled for DES-only Kerberos encryption

remediation.summary: Clear the 'Use Kerberos DES encryption types for this account' flag on every account.
steps: Review each account reported here.
In the account's properties, clear 'Use Kerberos DES encryption types for this account', then reset its password.
remediation.risk: DES is broken and its tickets are trivially crackable; a rare legacy device that only speaks DES loses Kerberos when the flag is cleared.

references.title: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets

indicators.title: Domain Admins has more than 10 members

remediation.summary: Reduce Domain Admins to the few accounts that administer domain controllers; delegate everything else.
steps: Review each member (direct and nested) with its owner.
Delegate specific tasks through OU permissions or Just-Enough-Administration groups.
Remove members that do not administer domain controllers.
remediation.risk: Removing a member that performs a task nobody delegated yet interrupts that task.

references.title: Best Practices for Securing Active Directory — reducing the attack surface
Valid Accounts: Domain Accounts

indicators.title: Schema Admins or Enterprise Admins have permanent members

remediation.summary: Keep Schema Admins and Enterprise Admins empty and add members only for the duration of a change.
steps: Remove every member except the forest root built-in Administrator.
Add an account temporarily when a schema or forest-wide change is planned, and remove it afterwards.
remediation.risk: Forest-wide changes planned for the same window need a member added first.

references.title: Appendix E: Securing Enterprise Admins Groups

indicators.title: The Protected Users group is empty

remediation.summary: Add privileged user accounts to Protected Users after testing.
steps: Test with one administrative account: Protected Users blocks NTLM, DES/RC4 and delegation for its members.
Add the remaining privileged user accounts (never service or computer accounts).
remediation.risk: Members cannot use NTLM or cached credentials; an admin that relies on them loses access.

references.title: Protected Users security group
Use Alternate Authentication Material: Pass the Ticket

indicators.title: Built-in operator groups (Account, Server, Print, Backup Operators) have members

remediation.summary: Empty the built-in operator groups and delegate the needed rights explicitly.
steps: Identify why each member was added (backups, printer management, account management).
Grant those specific rights through delegation or dedicated groups.
Remove the members from the built-in operator groups.
remediation.risk: Backup software running as a Backup Operators member fails until it is granted the equivalent rights.

references.title: Appendix B: Privileged Accounts and Groups in Active Directory

indicators.title: AdminSDHolder grants write access to non-default principals

remediation.summary: Review every non-default write ACE on AdminSDHolder and remove the ones nobody can justify.
steps: List the ACEs reported here (trustee and right).
Confirm with the owning team whether each one is a product requirement (for example Exchange).
Remove unjustified ACEs with 'dsacls' or ADSI Edit; SDProp re-applies the template to protected accounts within 60 minutes.
remediation.risk: Removing an ACE a product depends on breaks that product's management of privileged accounts.

references.title: Appendix C: Protected Accounts and Groups in Active Directory
Account Manipulation

indicators.title: Non-default principals hold replication rights on the domain (DCSync)

remediation.summary: Remove 'Replicating Directory Changes All' (and GenericAll) from every principal that is not a domain controller.
steps: Identify each trustee reported here.
If the trustee is the Microsoft Entra Connect sync account, keep it, restrict who can log on to the sync server and record an exception.
Remove the ACE for any other trustee from the domain root (dsacls <domainDN> /R <trustee>).
remediation.risk: Directory synchronization tools that legitimately read password hashes stop syncing if their right is removed.

references.title: OS Credential Dumping: DCSync

indicators.title: Non-default principals can reset passwords or take over privileged accounts

remediation.summary: Review every non-default principal that can reset the password of, or take ownership of, a protected account, and remove the rights nobody can justify.
steps: List the principals reported here and, for each, the right and an example account.
Confirm with the owning team whether each one is a product requirement (for example a PAM or password-reset tool).
Remove the ACE from AdminSDHolder (CN=AdminSDHolder,CN=System) so SDProp re-stamps every protected account within 60 minutes, or from the specific account for a one-off.
remediation.risk: Removing a right a delegated help-desk or PAM tool depends on breaks that workflow.

references.title: Account Manipulation
Protecting Tier 0 the modern way

indicators.title: Non-default principals can change the membership of privileged groups

remediation.summary: Remove the ability to write the membership of privileged groups from every principal that is not a default administrator.
steps: List the principals reported here and the groups they can modify.
Confirm whether each is a product requirement.
Remove 'Write Members' (or the broader right) from AdminSDHolder or the specific group.
remediation.risk: A group-management tool that legitimately writes membership stops working if its right is removed.

references.title: Account Manipulation
AdminSDHolder, Protected Groups and SDPROP

indicators.title: Non-default principals have dangerous control over domain controller objects

remediation.summary: Remove write control over domain controller computer objects from every non-default principal.
steps: List the principals reported here.
Confirm none is required (writing msDS-KeyCredentialLink on a DC allows a full takeover).
Remove the ACE from the affected domain controller objects.
remediation.risk: Write access to a DC computer object, especially its key credential link, is a path to Domain Admin; removing a legitimate management right can break that tool.

references.title: Exploitation of Remote Services
msDS-KeyCredentialLink / Shadow Credentials

indicators.title: Non-default principals can modify Group Policy Objects

remediation.summary: Remove edit rights on Group Policy Objects from every principal that is not a default administrator.
steps: List the principals and the GPOs they can edit.
Confirm whether the delegation is intended (a GPO admin team is legitimate).
Remove the delegation in the Group Policy Management Console if it is not.
remediation.risk: Edit rights on a GPO linked to domain controllers or Tier 0 is a path to full compromise; removing a legitimate GPO-admin delegation breaks that team.

references.title: Domain Policy Modification: Group Policy Modification

indicators.title: Non-default principals hold partial directory replication rights

remediation.summary: Review who holds 'Replicating Directory Changes' (or 'In Filtered Set') without also holding the 'All' right, and remove it where it is not needed.
steps: Identify each principal reported here.
A directory-sync tool (for example Microsoft Entra Connect) legitimately needs these rights: keep it, restrict logon to its server and record an exception.
Remove the right from any other principal on the domain root.
remediation.risk: Partial replication rights combined with other access can still be abused; removing a right a sync tool depends on stops synchronization.

references.title: OS Credential Dumping: DCSync

indicators.title: Enabled accounts keep adminCount=1 but are no longer in a protected group

remediation.summary: Restore inheritance and clear adminCount on accounts that are no longer privileged, so they stop carrying the restrictive AdminSDHolder ACL.
steps: Confirm each account is genuinely no longer privileged (it left every protected group).
Clear adminCount and re-enable ACL inheritance on the object (Enable-ADAccountInheritance or the object's Security tab).
If the account should still be privileged, add it back to the correct group instead.
remediation.risk: An orphaned adminCount object keeps a hardened ACL that blocks normal delegation; clearing it on a still-privileged account would remove that protection.

references.title: AdminSDHolder, Protected Groups and SDPROP

indicators.title: Non-default principals can write delegation or key credentials on the krbtgt account

remediation.summary: Remove every non-default write permission on the krbtgt account.
steps: List the principals reported here and the right each one holds.
None of them should exist: krbtgt is only written by the system and by domain administrators.
Remove the ACE (dsacls on the krbtgt DN) and, if the right was ever used, reset the krbtgt password twice as in ASP-AD-KRB-001.
remediation.risk: Writing delegation or key credentials on krbtgt hands over the key that signs every Kerberos ticket in the domain. Removing an ACE here breaks nothing legitimate.

references.title: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: Golden Ticket
AD Forest Recovery — Resetting the krbtgt password

indicators.title: Non-default principals can write userAccountControl at the domain root

remediation.summary: Remove the ability to write userAccountControl (or the User-Account-Restrictions property set) delegated at the domain root.
steps: Identify each principal reported here.
Writing userAccountControl on a computer allows setting SERVER_TRUST_ACCOUNT, which makes that computer a domain controller; it also allows clearing 'password required' on accounts.
Remove the delegation at the domain root, or narrow it to the specific OU and attributes the tool really needs.
remediation.risk: An account-provisioning tool delegated at the domain root can legitimately hold this right; removing it breaks that tool. This indicator only sees delegation at the DOMAIN ROOT — a delegation granted per OU is not covered.

references.title: Valid Accounts: Domain Accounts
userAccountControl flags

indicators.title: Privileged objects or domain controllers are owned by a non-administrator

remediation.summary: Set the owner of every privileged object and domain controller back to Domain Admins (or Administrators).
steps: Review each owner reported here and how many objects it owns.
The owner of an object can rewrite its permissions at will, so an unprivileged owner is equivalent to full control.
Change the owner to Domain Admins on the object's Security tab (Advanced > Owner), or with Set-Acl.
remediation.risk: An object created by a delegated admin keeps that account as owner, so this can be a legitimate side effect of provisioning; changing the owner does not break the object.

references.title: Account Manipulation
Appendix C: Protected Accounts and Groups in Active Directory

indicators.title: Membership of a privileged group changed in the last 7 days

remediation.summary: Confirm every recent addition to a privileged group was requested and approved, and remove the ones that were not.
steps: Read the evidence: each entry says which account was added or removed, when, and from which domain controller.
Match each change against your change record or ticket.
Remove any membership that nobody can account for, then reset the password of the account that made the change if it was not authorised.
remediation.risk: None: reviewing membership changes does not alter the directory. Removing a legitimate member breaks that person's access.

references.title: Account Manipulation
Understanding Active Directory replication metadata (msDS-ReplAttributeMetaData / msDS-ReplValueMetaData)
Change-detection indicators built on AD replication metadata

indicators.title: The AdminSDHolder permissions changed in the last 90 days

remediation.summary: Establish who changed the AdminSDHolder security descriptor and why: SDProp copies it onto every protected account within the hour.
steps: Read the evidence: it gives the write time, the version number and the domain controller that originated it.
Compare the current permissions against your documented baseline (indicator ASP-AD-PRV-005 lists the non-default principals).
If the change was not authorised, remove the added principals and treat every protected account as potentially compromised.
remediation.risk: None: this only reads metadata. Removing a legitimate delegation breaks whatever tool relied on it.

references.title: Account Manipulation
Understanding Active Directory replication metadata (msDS-ReplAttributeMetaData / msDS-ReplValueMetaData)
Change-detection indicators built on AD replication metadata

indicators.title: The domain permissions changed in the last 90 days

remediation.summary: Establish who changed the permissions on the domain object: this is where replication (DCSync) rights are granted.
steps: Read the evidence: write time, version and originating domain controller.
Cross-check with ASP-AD-PRV-006, which lists the principals that currently hold replication rights.
If the change was not authorised, remove the added rights and rotate the krbtgt password twice, seven days apart.
remediation.risk: None: this only reads metadata.

references.title: OS Credential Dumping: DCSync
Understanding Active Directory replication metadata (msDS-ReplAttributeMetaData / msDS-ReplValueMetaData)
Change-detection indicators built on AD replication metadata

indicators.title: The krbtgt account was modified in the last 7 days

remediation.summary: Nothing should write to krbtgt except a deliberate password reset. Establish what changed and who changed it.
steps: Read the evidence: it names the attribute, the write time and the originating domain controller.
A change to msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity on krbtgt is an attack, not an administrative action: treat the domain as compromised.
A change to nTSecurityDescriptor means someone was granted rights over krbtgt — cross-check ASP-AD-PRV-013.
remediation.risk: None: this only reads metadata. Note that a legitimate krbtgt password reset does NOT appear here — that writes pwdLastSet, which this indicator does not watch.

indicators.title: The forest-wide dSHeuristics setting changed in the last 90 days

remediation.summary: dSHeuristics is a single forest-wide string that turns on anonymous LDAP among other things. Establish who changed it and why.
steps: Read the evidence for the write time and the originating domain controller.
Check the current value with ASP-AD-CFG-001: the third character enables anonymous LDAP operations when it is 2.
If the change was not authorised, restore the documented value — a wrong character here changes behaviour for the whole forest.
remediation.risk: None: this only reads metadata. Editing dSHeuristics affects every domain in the forest.

indicators.title: A published certificate template lets an unprivileged requester choose the subject and issue without approval (ESC1)

remediation.summary: Remove the requester's ability to supply the subject, or require manager approval, or restrict enrolment to administrators. Any one of the three closes it.
steps: Certificate Templates console -> the template -> Subject Name: choose 'Build from this Active Directory information' instead of 'Supply in the request'.
Or Issuance Requirements -> tick 'CA certificate manager approval'.
Or Security -> remove Enroll from the unprivileged principal named in the evidence.
Then reissue: the templates already issued stay valid, so revoke any certificate you cannot account for.
remediation.risk: Applications that legitimately supply their own subject stop enrolling. Check with the owner of the template before changing it.

references.title: Steal or Forge Authentication Certificates

indicators.title: An unprivileged principal can modify a published certificate template (ESC4)

remediation.summary: Whoever can rewrite a template can turn it into ESC1 and then request a certificate as anybody. Remove the write access.
steps: Certificate Templates console -> the template -> Security: remove Full Control, Write, Modify Permissions and Modify Owner from the principal named in the evidence.
Check the template's current settings too: it may already have been modified (indicator ASP-AD-PKI-001).
Confirm the owner of the template object is an administrator (ASP-AD-PRV-015 covers owners of privileged objects).
remediation.risk: A delegated team that legitimately manages templates loses that ability. Move them to a group you can audit instead of leaving the direct grant.

references.title: Steal or Forge Authentication Certificates

indicators.title: A published certificate template issues for any purpose or as an enrolment agent, without approval (ESC2 / ESC3)

remediation.summary: A certificate valid for any purpose, or one that lets the holder enrol on behalf of others, must not be issuable without approval by an unprivileged principal.
steps: Certificate Templates console -> the template -> Extensions -> Application Policies: replace 'Any Purpose' with the purposes the template actually needs.
For an enrolment agent template, require manager approval or restrict Enroll to the accounts that operate the agent.
Or Security -> remove Enroll from the unprivileged principal named in the evidence.
remediation.risk: Whatever relied on the broad purpose stops working. An enrolment agent template is often used by a real service: find it before removing the right.

references.title: Steal or Forge Authentication Certificates

indicators.title: Non-default principals can modify the certification authority objects or the NTAuth store (ESC5)

remediation.summary: Remove write access to the CA objects and to the NTAuth certificate store from every principal that is not a forest administrator.
steps: List the principals reported here and which object each one can modify.
Writing these objects allows publishing a rogue CA certificate into NTAuth, after which certificates signed by it authenticate to the whole forest.
Remove the permission with ADSI Edit on the object under CN=Public Key Services,CN=Services,CN=Configuration.
remediation.risk: This is forest-wide: a rogue certificate in NTAuth is trusted by every domain. Removing a permission an enterprise PKI tool depends on breaks that tool.

indicators.title: The Cert Publishers group contains accounts that are not certification authority computers

remediation.summary: Leave only the CA computer accounts in Cert Publishers.
steps: Review the members reported here: this group should hold the computer accounts of the certification authorities and nothing else.
Remove every user or group that is not a CA computer account.
remediation.risk: A member of Cert Publishers can publish certificates into the directory's user objects. Removing a CA's own computer account would break certificate publication, which is why only non-computer members are reported.

indicators.title: A privileged account has key credentials that could be used to authenticate as it (Shadow Credentials)

remediation.summary: A key credential lets its holder obtain a Kerberos ticket as the account without knowing the password. Confirm each one belongs to the person, and remove the ones that do not.
steps: ⚠️ Read this first: Windows Hello for Business writes this attribute legitimately, so a match is not automatically an attack. What you are looking for is an entry nobody can account for.
For each account in the evidence, check with the owner whether they enrolled a Windows Hello or FIDO2 credential.

Inspect the entries: Get-ADUser <account> -Properties msDS-KeyCredentialLink. Remove an unexplained one by clearing the attribute, then reset the account's password — the attacker may already hold a ticket.
Put privileged accounts in the Protected Users group (indicator ASP-AD-PRV-003) so their credentials are not cached.
remediation.risk: Clearing the attribute breaks Windows Hello for Business sign-in for that account until the user re-enrols. Confirm before removing.

indicators.title: A privileged account accepts an explicit certificate mapping (altSecurityIdentities)

remediation.summary: An explicit certificate mapping lets whoever holds a matching certificate sign in as the account. Confirm each mapping is intended and that it is a strong one.
steps: For each account in the evidence, read the mapping: Get-ADUser <account> -Properties altSecurityIdentities.

⚠️ A mapping by subject or issuer alone is WEAK: anyone who can get a certificate with that subject from any trusted issuer can sign in as the account. Since KB5014754 the strong forms are X509IssuerSerialNumber and X509SKI.
Replace a weak mapping with a strong one, or remove it if nobody can account for it, and then reset the account's password.
If the mapping exists for a smart card, the implicit mapping is usually enough and the explicit one can go.
remediation.risk: Removing a mapping that a real smart card or service relies on locks that sign-in out. Identify the owner first.

indicators.title: The krbtgt account has key credentials (never legitimate)

remediation.summary: Nothing legitimate writes a key credential to krbtgt. Treat the domain as compromised.
steps: krbtgt does not sign in, so there is no Windows Hello or smart card explanation: this is persistence.
Clear msDS-KeyCredentialLink on krbtgt.
Reset the krbtgt password TWICE, at least 7 days apart (waiting for replication between the two), and expect all Kerberos tickets to be reissued.
Find out who wrote it: indicator ASP-AD-CHG-004 reads the replication metadata of krbtgt and gives the date and the originating domain controller.
Review who holds write access over krbtgt (ASP-AD-PRV-013) before you finish.
remediation.risk: Resetting krbtgt twice invalidates every Kerberos ticket in the domain; do it in a maintenance window. Not doing it leaves the attacker able to forge tickets.

indicators.title: A group managed service account has not changed its password in more than 90 days

remediation.summary: A gMSA exists so its password rotates on its own. One that has not rotated in 90 days is either not rotating or not being used at all — and both are worth knowing.
steps: ⚠️ Read this first: gMSA rotation is LAZY. The password changes when a member host next retrieves it, so an old date can mean «nobody is using this account» rather than «rotation is broken». The two need different actions.
Check the interval: Get-ADServiceAccount <name> -Properties msDS-ManagedPasswordInterval, pwdLastSet. If pwdLastSet is much older than the interval, no member has retrieved the password.
If the account is in use, confirm the hosts in PrincipalsAllowedToRetrieveManagedPassword can reach a domain controller and that the service is actually running as the gMSA.
If nobody uses it, delete it: an unused account with a static password is the thing gMSA was meant to remove.
remediation.risk: Deleting a gMSA that some forgotten service still uses stops that service. Confirm with the service owner first.

indicators.title: A group managed service account keeps its password for longer than 90 days

remediation.summary: The rotation interval was raised above the 30-day default. A gMSA password that lives a year is a static password with extra steps.
steps: Read the current value: Get-ADServiceAccount <name> -Properties msDS-ManagedPasswordInterval.
⚠️ The interval cannot be changed on an existing gMSA: it is set at creation. Lowering it means creating a new gMSA and moving the service to it.
Unless something documented requires a long interval, create the replacement with the default (30 days) and retire this one.
remediation.risk: Moving a service to a new gMSA needs a restart of that service and a change to whatever grants it rights.

references.title: Group Managed Service Accounts overview

indicators.title: A group managed service account is a member of a privileged group

remediation.summary: Everyone listed in the account's PrincipalsAllowedToRetrieveManagedPassword can retrieve its password — so a privileged gMSA makes every one of those hosts privileged too.
steps: List who can retrieve the password: Get-ADServiceAccount <name> -Properties PrincipalsAllowedToRetrieveManagedPassword.
Every host and principal on that list is effectively a member of the privileged group. Decide whether that is really intended.
Prefer granting the gMSA exactly the rights its service needs instead of putting it in a privileged group.
If it must stay privileged, narrow PrincipalsAllowedToRetrieveManagedPassword to the smallest set of hosts and treat those hosts as tier-0.
remediation.risk: Removing the gMSA from the group breaks whatever its service does with those rights. Find out what it needs before changing the membership.

indicators.title: Everyone in a broad group can retrieve a group managed service account's password

remediation.summary: PrincipalsAllowedToRetrieveManagedPassword names a group like Domain Users or Domain Computers, so anyone in it can read the password and act as the service.
steps: See the full list in the evidence, or: Get-ADServiceAccount <name> -Properties PrincipalsAllowedToRetrieveManagedPassword.
Create a dedicated group holding only the hosts that run the service, and set it as the only retriever: Set-ADServiceAccount <name> -PrincipalsAllowedToRetrieveManagedPassword <that group>.
⚠️ Domain Computers counts as broad on purpose: by default any user can join up to 10 computers to the domain (ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota), and each of those can then retrieve the password.
The hosts must refresh their Kerberos ticket before the change applies to them; restart the service (or the host) and check it still starts.
remediation.risk: A host that ran the service but is left out of the new group stops being able to start it. List the hosts using the account before narrowing it.

indicators.title: An unprivileged user account can retrieve a group managed service account's password

remediation.summary: Retrievers are normally the hosts that run the service. A person's account on the list can read the password and use the service's rights from anywhere.
steps: Check the evidence: each match names the user account and every other retriever of the same gMSA.
If the user was added to test or install the service, remove it: Set-ADServiceAccount <name> -PrincipalsAllowedToRetrieveManagedPassword <only the hosts or host group>.
If a person genuinely needs it, prefer a dedicated administrative account, and record an exception with the reason.
remediation.risk: Low: the service keeps working as long as its hosts stay on the list. Only the user loses access to the password.

indicators.title: Non-default principals can link Group Policy Objects at the domain root

remediation.summary: Linking a GPO at the domain root applies its settings to every computer and user in the domain. Whoever can write gPLink there can push code or settings everywhere.
steps: Check who is named in the evidence and why they can write gPLink on the domain root.

Remove the delegation (Active Directory Users and Computers -> Advanced Features -> Security on the object, or Delegation in Group Policy Management) unless it is a documented GPO-administration role.
If the role is real, grant it to a dedicated group that you audit, not to individual accounts.
remediation.risk: Whoever manages Group Policy through that delegation loses the ability to link GPOs there. Confirm with the GPO administrators first.

indicators.title: A linked Group Policy Object grants dangerous user rights to non-default principals

remediation.summary: Rights such as Debug programs, Act as part of the operating system, Back up / Restore files or Load device drivers give their holder SYSTEM-level control of every computer the GPO applies to.
steps: The evidence names the GPO, where it is linked, the right and the principal. An entry marked as not resolved is a name the GPO could not translate to a SID when it was written: find out what it is.
Group Policy Management -> the GPO -> Computer Configuration -> Policies -> Windows Settings -> Security Settings -> Local Policies -> User Rights Assignment: remove the principal from the right.
If a service genuinely needs it (for example a backup product), grant it to that service's account only, and record an exception with the reason.
remediation.risk: The service or person that relied on the right stops working on the computers in scope. Identify who uses it before removing it.

indicators.title: A linked Group Policy Object puts a broad group into a privileged local group

remediation.summary: Restricted Groups in this GPO make a group like Domain Users or Authenticated Users a member of Administrators (or another privileged local group) on every computer in scope — and on a domain controller, the local Administrators group is the domain's.
steps: Group Policy Management -> the GPO -> Computer Configuration -> Policies -> Windows Settings -> Security Settings -> Restricted Groups: remove the broad group from the privileged group.
If people need local administration, use LAPS or a dedicated, audited group per tier instead.
Check where the GPO is linked (in the evidence): if it reaches domain controllers, treat the domain as exposed until it is fixed.
remediation.risk: Users who relied on being local administrators lose it. Plan for the software installs or support tasks they used it for.

indicators.title: A linked Group Policy Object stores passwords with reversible encryption

remediation.summary: With 'Store passwords using reversible encryption' enabled, every password changed afterwards in scope is stored in a form that can be turned back into the clear-text password.
steps: Group Policy Management -> the GPO -> Computer Configuration -> Policies -> Windows Settings -> Security Settings -> Account Policies -> Password Policy: set 'Store passwords using reversible encryption' to Disabled.
Passwords already stored that way stay recoverable until they are changed: force a change for the accounts in scope (ASP-AD-ACC-002 lists accounts with the flag set directly).
remediation.risk: Applications that authenticate with CHAP or Digest authentication against those accounts stop working. They are rare; check before changing.

indicators.title: A linked Group Policy Object allows anonymous SID and name translation

remediation.summary: 'Allow anonymous SID/Name translation' lets an unauthenticated caller turn SIDs into account names, which is enough to enumerate the domain's administrators.
steps: Group Policy Management -> the GPO -> Computer Configuration -> Policies -> Windows Settings -> Security Settings -> Local Policies -> Security Options: set 'Network access: Allow anonymous SID/Name translation' to Disabled.
remediation.risk: Very old clients or appliances that look up names anonymously stop resolving them. Rare on supported systems.
